To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin reduces, but does not eliminate, the injury-induced synaptic reorganization in hilar inhibitory inter-neurons.

the mTOR pathway is involved in the injury-induced plastic changes in hippocampal inhibitory interneuron circuits, and that mTOR inhibition does not fully suppress the injury-induced plastic alterations in the excitability of these cells.

the excitability of somatostatin-expressing interneurons is increased after TBI, but that this injury-induced increase in synaptic input from both granule cells and CA3 pyramids is differentially affected by rapamycin.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms underlying epileptogenesis, the process that leads to the development of spontaneous seizures following brain trauma.
the mechanisms underlying the reorganization of hippocampal inhibitory circuits in response to brain injury, and the effects of mTOR inhibition upon that reorganization.
the mechanisms of epilepsy after traumatic brain injury (TBIE).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
mTOR inhibition suppresses some, but not all, components of the synaptic reorganization that occurs after TBI.
rapamycin treatment suppresses some but not all aspects of synaptic reorganization and that the incomplete suppression could contribute to incomplete control of epileptogenesis.

rapamycin treatment reduces the injury-induced increase of excitability of somatostatin-positive hilar interneurons, and the injury-induced increase synaptic excitation arising in these interneurons from dentate granule cells, while the injury-induced increase excitatory input from CA3 pyramids is unaffected.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the injury-induced increase excitability of hilar interneurons is partially normalized by mTOR inhibition, which is associated with a selective reduction in excitatory input from DGCs, but not CA3 pyramids.

the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin can suppress synaptic reorganization in the hilar inhibitory neurons after TBI, but this suppression is incomplete and does not prevent reemergence and recurrence of seizures after cessation.

the effect of mTOR on synaptic reorganization in hilar inhibitory neurons is differentially affected after brain injury and that the injury-induced increase of synaptic input from CA3 neurons is not affected by mTOR inhibition.
The main takeaway from our work is that
mTOR inhibition can reduce the excitability of hippocampal inhibitory neurons after TBI.

mTOR inhibition does not completely normalize the injury-induced increase of synaptic excitation onto hilar interneurons after TBI, which may contribute to the reemergence and progression of epileptogenesis in the injured hippocampus.
the effect of rapamycin on synaptic reorganization in the hippocampus is cell-type specific.
